prompt.context: Six months out of Wharton a frustrated classmate calls you to complain that the fast food burger joint that he bought has been steadily losing money for the last 3 months. He wants to know what you think he should do about it.
prompt.question: Where do you start? What would you do to diagnose and address the problem?

clarifying_info.q: What do you mean by losing money — have profits declined or is the business in the red?
Have revenues decreased, costs increased, or both?
Are there fewer paying customers, or are customers spending less per visit?
Is the issue primarily internal (food quality, prices, health incident) or external (competition, economic change)?
clarifying_info.a: The issue is external and is driven by a new competitor that opened across the street.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitor's value proposition — different food, better quality, lower prices?
clarifying_info.a: They serve chicken dinners and appear to offer a completely different dining experience.

framework: Define the problem: clarify whether the business is losing money overall or whether profits have simply declined
Decompose P&L: separate revenue decline from cost increase — identify which driver is primary
Revenue breakdown: fewer customers vs. lower spend per customer
Customer volume root cause: external factors (new competition, area economic change, shift in eating habits) vs. internal factors (food quality, price increase, health incident, crime)
Competitive analysis: visit competitor firsthand to assess food quality, price, variety, service, facility, parking, and access
Internal audit: apply the same lens to the burger joint to benchmark relative value proposition
Primary research: customer interviews at both locations to measure perception gaps and understand switching behavior
Option generation and prioritization: identify improvement levers (menu, facility, quality, price), score by expected traffic impact and ROI, then build a sequenced action plan

questions.prompt: Walk through your initial diagnostic framework for a business that is losing money.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates immediately structure around revenue vs. cost, then drill into revenue (volume vs. price) and cost (fixed vs. variable). They ask clarifying questions in a logical order before hypothesizing.

questions.prompt: Revenues have fallen because there are fewer customers. What could explain that?
questions.guidance: Candidate should distinguish external causes (new competition, area business closing, demographic shifts, macro change) from internal causes (food quality, pricing, health code violation, crime). Framing both buckets before diving shows structure.

questions.prompt: The cause is a new chicken restaurant across the street. How would you get a deep understanding of their value proposition?
questions.guidance: First-hand visit to assess: food quality, price, menu variety and healthier options, service speed and friendliness, cleanliness, facility layout, parking and ease of access. Then mirror the same audit on the burger joint to compare. Follow with primary research: pay customers to visit both locations and rate the experience; identify what share of customers are defectors, dual visitors, or net-new to the chicken restaurant.

questions.prompt: Armed with competitive intelligence and customer data, how do you develop an action plan?
questions.guidance: Generate a set of options (new menu items, facility upgrades, quality improvement, pricing adjustment, marketing/promotion). Evaluate each option against criteria: expected traffic recovery speed and ROI. Prioritize, then build an action plan with clear timing and ownership.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should you investigate when a restaurant's customer count has declined?

categories.name: External — Competition
ideas: New competitor nearby offering better value or different cuisine
Competitor running a promotional campaign or price war

categories.name: External — Market/Area
ideas: Major local employer closed, reducing foot traffic
General economic downturn affecting discretionary spend

categories.name: Internal — Product
ideas: Decline in food quality or consistency
Menu no longer meeting customer preferences
Lack of healthier or more varied options

categories.name: Internal — Operations
ideas: Slower service or longer wait times
Decline in cleanliness or facility condition
Staff attitude or customer service deterioration

categories.name: Internal — Pricing
ideas: Price increase not matched by perceived value
Competitor offering better value at similar or lower price

categories.name: Internal — Reputation
ideas: Health code violation or food safety incident
Negative press, social media reviews, or word of mouth
Crime incident near or at the location

recommendation: Conduct firsthand competitive assessment of the chicken restaurant and an honest internal audit of the burger joint to quantify the value gap
Run structured customer interviews at both locations to identify the top two or three experience gaps that are driving defection

Prioritize and execute the highest-impact, fastest-ROI improvement levers — likely starting with menu variety and service quality — before considering more capital-intensive options like facility renovation
risks: Improvement investments may not recoup customers already habituated to the new competitor
If the burger joint lacks differentiation beyond burgers in a market shifting toward variety, the structural headwind may persist regardless of operational fixes
Capital constraints may limit the owner's ability to execute multiple initiatives simultaneously
next_steps: Visit competitor and complete side-by-side audit within one week
Commission brief customer intercept survey at both locations
Build a prioritized options matrix with cost, timeline, and expected traffic lift for each initiative
Set a 90-day revenue target to evaluate whether the turnaround plan is working
